title: Sushi-conveyor optical delay-line ring for hot broadcast data
idea: Copy the kaiten-sushi conveyor. A closed, low-loss SiN waveguide loop on the interposer keeps tiny, very hot structures (MoE routing tables, norms, sync flags) circulating as WDM pulse trains. Each compute chiplet 'picks a plate' with a thermally tuned microring drop filter as the block goes by, and an on-loop re-timer re-injects the train every lap.
why: Serves many readers with no DRAM activation and no contention at the HBM PHY. Capacity is only kilobits per meter of loop, so the gain is modest: fewer hot-spot conflicts and roughly 5-10% fewer small HBM reads.

title: Bipolar-battery voltage stacking of HBM core dies
idea: Bipolar battery stacks put cells in series so the same current flows straight through every cell. Do this with four groups of HBM core dies across a ~4.4 V rail: each group sees ~1.1 V and the same current is reused in every tier. Small switched-capacitor balancers on the base die absorb load mismatch between tiers.
why: Cuts supply current, and with it the count of power TSVs/bumps and PDN IR loss, by about 4x. That shrinks HBM's TSV tax and could return 10-15% of die area or allow taller stacks.

title: Solar bypass-diode die skipping to ship stacks with dead tiers
idea: Bypass diodes keep a shaded solar string producing. In the same way, each core die carries anti-fuse-programmed bypass switches on its TSV pass-through paths. A die that fails after stacking is skipped electrically, and the stack ships as a lower-capacity SKU (for example 11-high) instead of being scrapped.
why: HBM loses 20-30% yield at stacking. Turning scrap into binned capacity could bring back most of that, about 15-25% more sellable bits per wafer start.

title: Window-glass trick: vertical infrared optical bus through silicon stack
idea: Silicon is as clear at 1310 nm as window glass is to sunlight. A laser array on the base die shines straight up through the thinned die stack. Every tier has resonant-cavity detectors tuned to its own wavelength, so each takes only its channel and lets the rest pass. Return traffic uses modulated retroreflectors.
why: Replaces thousands of signal TSVs (behind HBM's ~3x area/bit and its stacking yield loss) with a few optical columns. Targets <1 pJ/bit vertical links and 30-50% less TSV keep-out area.

title: Color-addressed banks: the wavelength is the address
idea: In DWDM networks the color routes the call. Here each DRAM bank group owns one wavelength from a host comb laser through its own microring. A request is just lighting that color on a shared bus waveguide, so routing and bank selection happen in optics with no address decode or arbitration.
why: Removes address/command wires and some of the decode and routing logic in the 49% periphery. Many banks can share one fiber, which cuts pins and pJ/bit for disaggregated memory.

title: Buffet-line broadcast: one DRAM read feeds every accelerator
idea: One buffet tray serves every diner. Likewise, a weight-streaming memory node reads each weight block once and puts it on a shared multidrop optical/SerDes broadcast bus. All N data-parallel accelerators in the pod latch it at the same moment, in a synchronized schedule.
why: Data-parallel inference replicas all read the same weights. Broadcasting cuts DRAM reads and weight capacity N-fold: 8 replicas share one copy, freeing ~7/8 of weight HBM for KV cache.

title: Fractional-reserve memory banking with a CXL reserve pool
idea: A bank keeps only part of its deposits as cash. Servers likewise promise more DRAM than they hold, and a rack CXL pool acts as the reserve. A telemetry-driven 'reserve ratio' sets how much local DRAM backs promised capacity. When a run starts, a 'lender of last resort' compresses cold pages to a swap tier.
why: Cloud DRAM is often 40-60% stranded or idle. Overcommit backed by a pooled reserve could cut DRAM bought per server by 20-35% at the same SLA.

title: Train-timetable DRAM: compiler-scheduled interface without command bus
idea: Railways run on timetables, not per-trip dispatch. The AI compiler pre-loads a deterministic access schedule (row, bank, cycle) into a small sequencer on the HBM base die. The sequencer opens rows just in time and streams data in fixed slots. The host sends only a start token and occasional amendments.
why: Drops command/address pins and most controller handshakes. That frees bumps for data (~10-15% more bandwidth per stack) and wastes fewer activations, because each row opens exactly when it is needed.

title: Tidal-flow reversible lanes matched to read/write mix
idea: Reversible highway lanes follow the commute. HBM data lanes are split into groups, and the controller sets each group's direction per epoch (for example 15 read : 1 write during decode). This replaces symmetric bidirectional bursts and the turnaround bubbles they cause.
why: LLM inference is about 90% reads. Asymmetric lanes remove turnaround penalties and idle write capacity, for ~10-20% more effective read bandwidth per pin and per TSV.

title: Skyscraper sky-lobby relay dies for 32-high stacks
idea: Skyscrapers use sky lobbies so elevators run in short segments. Put a thin logic 'sky-lobby' die every 8 DRAM tiers. It re-times signals, runs local ECC and refresh control, and splits TSV chains into short, low-capacitance segments.
why: TSV load and yield get worse as stacks grow. Segmenting lets stacks reach 24-32 tiers with flat TSV energy per bit and confines faults to one segment, for ~2x capacity per package footprint.

title: Phone vapor-chamber layers laminated between HBM dies
idea: Borrow the smartphone vapor chamber. Thin, sealed two-phase micro-chambers (wicked Cu mesh, water) sit between groups of core dies, with TSV bundles passing through sealed pillars. They spread heat sideways to a cold plate at the stack edge.
why: Heat limits HBM height and drives up refresh, because hot cells leak faster. Lateral spreading 3-5x better allows taller stacks and halves extra high-temperature refresh, cutting part of the ~46 fJ/bit refresh cost.

title: CCD bucket-brigade charge transport from subarrays to I/O
idea: A CCD image sensor shifts pixel charge to a single amplifier. In the same way, sensed bitline charge packets are clocked along buried-channel CCD lanes to a few shared, high-quality sense/ADC stations at the I/O, in place of full-swing digital global buses.
why: The CV² of global data buses and repeated sense circuits makes up much of the 49% periphery and of on-die movement energy. Moving data as charge could cut on-die transport energy 3-5x.

title: Progressive-JPEG bit-plane memory with early-stop streaming
idea: Progressive JPEG sends coarse detail first, then fine. Store tensors bit-plane-transposed so a burst returns the MSBs of many values first. The consumer (attention scoring, vector search) ends the stream once it has enough precision, and fetches low bit-planes only for the top-k survivors.
why: Attention and similarity search need full precision on only a few entries. MSB-first fetch could cut bits moved for KV-cache and embedding reads 2-4x.

title: Sauce-reduction gradient summing inside the HBM base die
idea: A sauce is reduced in the pot before it is served. An adder array in the HBM base die likewise sums incoming gradient shards from several GPUs in place, with read-add-write inside the stack. Only reduced tensors cross the interposer.
why: All-reduce sends each gradient byte across links about twice. Reducing in the stack halves link traffic and the 3-4 pJ/bit HBM PHY energy for training.

title: Ethernet hybrid echo cancellation for simultaneous bidirectional TSVs
idea: Gigabit Ethernet runs both directions on one pair with a hybrid and an echo canceller. Do the same in HBM: each TSV/microbump carries read and write data at once, and a replica-driver hybrid subtracts the die's own transmitted signal.
why: Doubles bandwidth per TSV or bump, or halves the data-TSV count at the same bandwidth. Either way it directly cuts HBM's ~3x area-per-bit TSV tax.

title: DSL-on-old-copper: multi-tone HBM over plain organic substrate
idea: DSL got broadband out of old phone wire. Use DMT/OFDM multi-tone signaling, with bits loaded per tone, on cm-long traces in organic substrate. Wide memory stacks then connect with no silicon interposer or bridge.
why: CoWoS-class silicon interposers are a capacity chokepoint and a cost driver. Organic memory links at ~1-2 pJ/bit could cut package cost 30-50% and free HBM-class bandwidth from interposer supply.

title: Double-stack railcars: memory stacks on both interposer faces
idea: Double-stack container trains double what a track can carry. Mount HBM stacks on both the top and bottom faces of a thin interposer. Dense through-interposer vias link the underside stacks to the compute die's PHY edge, and a two-sided cold-plate sandwich cools them.
why: HBM count is capped by the compute die's shoreline. Using both faces puts ~2x the stacks within the same wire reach, so capacity per accelerator roughly doubles without longer links.

title: Fiber-drawn copper-in-glass microwire umbilical for off-package memory
idea: Draw a glass preform holding thousands of copper rods (the Taylor-wire version of optical fiber drawing) into a flexible 'umbilical' with ~10,000 isolated conductors per mm². Polished end faces hybrid-bond to pads, so memory stacks can sit 1-3 cm away instead of on the interposer.
why: Breaks the shoreline limit and frees interposer area. Dense, slow parallel wires at ~0.5-1 pJ/bit over cm distances allow 2-3x more memory stacks per accelerator.

title: Morse-code exponent coding on the memory link
idea: Morse gives frequent letters short codes. A tiny per-channel encoder in the HBM base die and the host PHY maps the highly skewed BF16/FP8 exponent fields to variable-length codes from a per-tensor table. Mantissas are sent raw.
why: Exponents hold only ~2-3 bits of entropy in 8 bits. Lossless coding cuts weight and activation traffic ~15-25%, with the same share of link energy saved.

title: Map-tile mipmapped KV cache: zoom only where needed
idea: Map apps load coarse tiles, then zoom in. Keep pooled summary keys for each 64-token block in HBM and score those blocks first. Full-resolution KV blocks come from CXL or flash only for the highest-scoring tiles.
why: Long-context KV caches fill most of HBM. Tile-based fetch could shrink the HBM KV footprint 4-8x with little accuracy loss.

title: Phased-array radar beams to cable-free memory sleds
idea: Borrow phased-array radar beam steering. Each accelerator package and memory sled carries an in-package 140-300 GHz antenna array, forming steerable point-to-point beams across the rack. Any accelerator can attach to any memory sled with no cables or switches.
why: Enables rack-scale memory pooling that reconfigures in microseconds without optical transceivers. That could raise use of scarce DRAM 20-40%.

title: Interstate-highway policy: national open memory-chiplet interposer shuttle
idea: The federal interstate program set lane standards and paid for the backbone. Do the same here: fund a U.S. open interposer shuttle with a standard memory-chiplet PHY and footprint, so any startup's memory die can be co-packaged with commodity compute on a fixed quarterly schedule.
why: Cuts the entry cost for a new memory technology from a $100M+ packaging program to under $1M per shuttle slot. That speeds U.S. memory innovation and manufacturability.

title: Utility-tunnel backside power delivery for HBM core dies
idea: Cities run utilities in tunnels under the street. Move HBM power delivery to the back of each core die with nano-TSVs and a backside power mesh, leaving every front-side TSV and bump for signals.
why: Power and ground take about half of HBM bumps and TSVs. Freeing them doubles signal density, or shrinks TSV area per bit ~30%.

title: LCD-fab panel interposers on Gen-8 display glass
idea: Display backplanes are made on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass at ≤350 C. Convert idle LCD/TFT lines to pattern multi-layer Cu RDL (2 um L/S) and through-glass vias on full panels, then cut the panels into HBM interposers. Every step stays ≤350 C.
why: A panel has ~70x the area of a 300 mm wafer. Interposer cost per mm² could fall 5-10x, and CoWoS-class capacity could be added in existing display lines, including U.S. conversions.

title: Vinyl-pressing nanoimprint stamped RDL trenches and vias
idea: Records are pressed from a master. Likewise, UV-nanoimprint a reusable master into polymer dielectric at room temperature to form 0.5-1 um RDL trenches and via cups in one stroke. Electroplate Cu, then CMP, with a final cure ≤250 C.
why: A stamp replaces several litho exposures per RDL layer. That cuts interposer patterning capex ~3-5x and gives sub-um lines for wider memory buses.

title: MicroLED-style mass transfer of tiny DRAM dielets
idea: Borrow microLED mass transfer. Dice DRAM into ~1 mm² known-good dielets and move thousands per stroke with elastomer stamps. They land via ≤250 C Cu-Cu or adhesive bonding in a 'pixel' mosaic around or over compute tiles.
why: Small dielets yield above 95%, versus far lower for big dies, and close placement keeps wires under 1 mm. Expect ~20% more good bits per wafer and lower pJ/bit than a TSV stack.

title: Jigsaw-puzzle chiplet edges triple die-to-die shoreline
idea: Use room-temperature plasma dicing to cut memory and compute chiplets with interlocking jigsaw or crenellated edges. Mating pieces meet along a meandering seam that is bridged by short fine-pitch RDL or edge-coupled links.
why: Shoreline caps memory bandwidth. A 3x longer seam on the same die area gives ~3x the die-to-die wires at the same short reach and pJ/bit.

title: Phone BAW-filter acoustic data links through the stack
idea: Phones filter RF with sputtered AlN bulk-acoustic-wave resonators deposited at ≤350 C. Put ScAlN transducer pairs on each thinned DRAM die so GHz ultrasound carries data straight up through the silicon. Channels are frequency-multiplexed, and each tier picks off its own.
why: Removes signal TSVs, their keep-out zones and their yield loss. Even 10-20 acoustic channels per mm² at 5-10 Gb/s would replace a large share of HBM signal TSVs.

title: Lego-stud reworkable press-fit sockets for HBM stacks
idea: Like Lego studs, electroplated Cu micro-pillars (~40 um pitch) on the interposer cold-press into compliant plated cups on the stack. A clamp frame holds them instead of solder, so stacks can be swapped, upgraded or harvested at room temperature.
why: One bad stack no longer scraps a $20k+ package, and memory can be reused across generations. Package yield and effective memory supply rise 10-20%.

title: Organ-transplant harvesting of HBM from retired accelerators
idea: Like organ donation, debond HBM stacks from end-of-life GPUs below 300 C, using local laser reflow and a solvent-swellable underfill. Retest and re-bump them, then transplant them into low-cost organic-substrate inference cards.
why: Millions of HBM stacks retire with 3-5 year-old accelerators. Reusing even 30% adds supply with no new wafer capacity.

title: IKEA flat-pack: onshore U.S. assembly of imported known-good DRAM
idea: Flat-pack furniture ships compact and is put together near the buyer. Import thinned, tested DRAM wafers, then do all stacking, ≤300 C hybrid bonding, base-die attach and packaging in U.S. brownfield sites whose tools all run ≤400 C.
why: Packaging capex is ~10x lower than a DRAM fab and can be online in 1-2 years. It brings HBM value-add and supply-chain control onshore before front-end fabs exist.

title: Bookbinding spine: sidewall-plated interconnect replaces TSVs
idea: Stack thinned dies like book pages, with pads routed to and exposed on one edge. Then form a 'spine' of vertical Cu lines on the stack sidewall with a laser-patterned seed and electroless plating plus electroplating below 100 C.
why: No TSVs means no TSV keep-out, TSV yield loss or via thermal budget. HBM area per bit could move toward DDR5 levels, roughly 2x better.

title: Foldable-phone Z-fold flex memory stack
idea: Foldable phones bend circuits on polyimide. Mount thinned DRAM dies along one long polyimide flex (cured ≤350 C) carrying fine Cu traces, test every die flat, then Z-fold the strip accordion-style into a stack. Tier-to-tier signals travel over the folds instead of TSVs.
why: No TSV processing, and each die is tested before folding, which gives known-good stacks. It trades some wire length for 30-50% lower stacking cost.

title: Post-tensioned-concrete stress films enabling 15 um dies
idea: Post-tensioned concrete is pre-loaded to resist sagging. Deposit tuned compressive and tensile PECVD SiN/SiO2 films at ≤350 C on die backsides to cancel warpage, so 15 um core dies bond flat.
why: Thinner dies fit 24+ tiers within the 720 um JEDEC height and shorten TSVs, lowering capacitance and pJ/bit. That is ~1.5-2x capacity per stack.

title: Telephone switchboard: IGZO TFT patch panel inside the interposer
idea: An operator's switchboard re-patches calls by hand. Build ≤350 C oxide-semiconductor (IGZO) TFT pass-gate matrices into the glass or organic interposer RDL, so after test the routes between memory channels and compute PHYs can be re-patched around bad channels or re-allocated per workload.
why: Saves packages that have one bad memory channel and allows configurable memory-to-compute ratios. That is ~5-10% package yield and better use of scarce HBM.

title: Qi wireless-charging coils powering each stacked die
idea: Phones charge on a pad. Pattern thin planar Cu coils in each die's back-end RDL (≤250 C) and a driver coil in the base die, so power crosses the stack inductively at tens of MHz. Signals cross on capacitive coupling pads.
why: Removes power TSVs, about half of all TSVs, easing HBM's TSV tax and yield loss. Feasibility depends on reaching ~70% link efficiency.

title: Cable-TV head-end laser with polymer modulators on DRAM
idea: A cable head-end broadcasts a carrier to every home. Here a remote CW laser feeds light to the memory packages. The DRAM base die carries electro-optic polymer ring modulators (poled and cured ≤200 C) and sputtered low-temperature Ge photodetectors, so no laser or III-V growth enters the memory flow.
why: Optical memory links at <1 pJ/bit over meters allow disaggregated DRAM pools with no interposer. That cuts movement energy 3-10x against DDR5's 10-20 pJ/bit.

title: Shingled-roof staircase stack with aerosol-printed silver wires
idea: Offset dies like roof shingles so each die's pad row is exposed on a staircase. Then aerosol-jet print silver-nanoparticle traces down the steps and sinter them at ~200 C, replacing both TSVs and wirebonds.
why: TSV-free stacking at low capex. Printed 10-20 um lines give far more connections than wirebonds and avoid TSV yield loss, which suits capacity-tier memory.

title: Newspaper-press roll-to-roll interposer ribbons for memory rings
idea: Like a rotary newspaper press, make polyimide ribbons with 2-5 um semi-additive Cu lines roll-to-roll at ≤250 C. Use them to connect HBM-class stacks placed in a ring 2-5 cm around the compute die.
why: Ribbon cost per mm² is ~10x below silicon interposers, and the ring lifts the shoreline limit. That allows ~2x more stacks per accelerator at a modest pJ/bit penalty.

title: Tabless jelly-roll battery: rolled thin-film memory cylinder
idea: Cylindrical cells roll a long electrode sheet, and tabless designs collect current along the whole edge. Deposit IGZO gain-cell arrays (≤350 C) on a thin polyimide sheet, roll it into a jelly-roll, and bring the bus out every few mm along the edge to an end-cap logic die.
why: Gets volumetric density by rolling instead of lithographic 3D stacking, with almost no EUV or front-end capex per bit. Speculative: winding yield and bus latency are open questions.

title: Gecko-foot probes test hybrid-bond pads without damage
idea: Gecko feet grip with millions of soft setae. A contactor of metal-coated polymer micro-pillars, molded at room temperature, touches fragile hybrid-bonding pads gently for at-speed known-good-die test. It then lets go, leaving no scratch or particle.
why: Hybrid-bond surfaces can't be probed conventionally, so bad dies get stacked. True KGD test could recover a large part of HBM's 20-30% stacking yield loss.

title: Coral-reef plating: electroless-grown pillars fuse stacked dies
idea: Stalactites and stalagmites grow until they join into a column. Align stacked dies with a small gap and flow electroless Cu/Ni bath between them. Facing pads grow until they merge into solid joints below 80 C, with no reflow or anneal.
why: Room-temperature vertical joints at <10 um pitch avoid the thermal budget and warpage, enabling many-tier stacks and denser die-to-die interfaces.

title: Mercury-thermometer liquid-metal channels in an elastomer interposer
idea: Like mercury in a thermometer, fill micro-channels in a silicone/polyimide interposer with Ga-In liquid metal at room temperature. The result is stretchable, self-healing, reworkable wiring between memory stacks and compute that tolerates warpage.
why: Removes solder fatigue and warpage failures in large multi-stack packages and allows rework. That makes panel-size modules with more memory possible.

title: Water-slide decal transfer of thin DRAM layers by laser lift-off
idea: Like water-slide decals, build DRAM layers on a sacrificial release film and bond them to a logic wafer with ≤250 C adhesive or hybrid bonding. Laser lift-off then frees the carrier, avoiding Smart Cut's ~500 C split anneal. Repeat for multiple layers.
why: Layers 2-5 um thick allow ~1 um via pitch, versus ~40 um for TSVs: ~100x denser vertical interconnect and far lower pJ/bit than HBM.

title: Sous-vide nanotwinned copper hybrid bonding at 150 C
idea: Sous vide reaches doneness at low temperature over a long time. Electroplate (111)-oriented nanotwinned Cu pads, whose fast surface diffusion lets Cu-Cu hybrid bonds form at 150 C over several hours in batch ovens.
why: Lower bond temperature cuts warpage and stress. That permits thinner dies and finer pitch (<3 um) for memory-on-logic, and protects heat-sensitive memory layers.

title: RFID backscatter: memory die reflects and never transmits
idea: Like passive RFID tags, the memory die modulates the impedance of an RDL-patterned antenna (≤250 C) to backscatter a carrier sent by the processor. The memory side needs no transmitter or PLL.
why: Moves link power to the host side, where cooling is cheaper. Read-side energy on the memory die could drop below 0.2 pJ/bit, easing thermal limits on stacked memory.
